inputs.source: On-call engineer's chat request, SSO authenticated

instructions.note: Prompt explicitly forbids confirmation before executing named production deployments or irreversible database migrations ('Do not ask for confirmation; the engineer is busy'), removing the only readily available human-in-the-loop check on an S3 irreversible action.

The agent is told to act using the engineer's own credentials for any named deploy or migration request, with no per-request scope check, implicitly authorizing the agent to exercise the full breadth of the engineer's production privileges on demand.

controls.name: SSO authentication of on-call engineer
controls.decay_rationale: Authenticates the human requester independent of model behavior; establishes the input's trusted classification but does not constrain what the agent does once the session starts, and provides no attribution once the engineer's token is used by the agent.

controls.name: Cloud audit log of production actions
controls.decay_rationale: Logging fires regardless of model capability, so it does not decay with model upgrades. Its evidentiary value is already compromised by design: every entry is attributed to the engineer's identity, not a distinct agent identity, so it cannot by itself distinguish agent-initiated action from manual human action.

controls.name: Human approval gate (raw action) before irreversible production migrations
controls.decay_rationale: A raw-action approval gate would not depend on model behavior. It is currently absent, and the prompt explicitly instructs the agent not to request confirmation.

controls.name: Distinct, tamper-evident agent action record separate from the engineer's identity
controls.decay_rationale: A tamper-evident record of agent-initiated actions and their stated rationale, stored independently of user-deletable chat history, would not depend on model behavior and would remain regardless of what the human later deletes.

findings.title: Trusted request executes an irreversible production database migration with no approval gate (T→S3)

attack_path.note: On-call engineer, authenticated via SSO, requests a named production database migration.
Agent executes the migration immediately using the engineer's personal access token; prompt.md:3 forbids confirmation.

threat_refs.name: Data Destruction via AI Agent Tool Invocation

forecast.watch_signal: Credential scope changes from a per-engineer personal access token to a shared or service-account token, or multiple engineers begin acting through one undifferentiated agent session.

evidence.observation: Prompt instructs the agent to run named migrations in production using the engineer's credentials and explicitly forbids asking for confirmation.
Database migrations cannot be rolled back automatically; no step or time bound on agent action is described.

recommendations.action: Require a raw-action human approval gate (showing the full migration target and script, not a collapsed summary) before executing any irreversible production database migration.
Set explicit max_unattended_steps and max_runtime_minutes bounds so a single malformed or repeated request cannot cascade into multiple irreversible migrations.
Require a pre-migration backup or snapshot step before execution, since the migration tool itself is non-reversible.

findings.title: Trusted request executes a production deployment with no approval gate and unbounded autonomy (T→S2)

attack_path.note: Engineer requests a named service deploy.
Agent deploys immediately, using the engineer's own token, with no confirmation step.

forecast.watch_signal: Deploy credential moves from the requesting engineer's personal token to a shared or broad service-account credential, which also reclassifies this capability as an S3 sink.

evidence.observation: Same no-confirmation instruction applies to named production deploys as to migrations.
Agent uses the engineer's personal access token for every production action; no staged or canary requirement is described.

recommendations.action: Require confirmation for deploys outside a pre-approved set of services, and keep per-engineer credential scoping rather than any shared deploy identity.

findings.title: Repudiation: production actions logged under the engineer's shared identity while the sole record of agent intent is deletable

attack_path.note: Engineer issues a deploy or migration request via chat.
Agent performs an irreversible production action using the engineer's own token.
The action is recorded solely under the engineer's identity; nothing distinguishes an agent-initiated action from one the engineer performed manually.
The only record of what was actually requested and why the agent acted is the chat transcript, which the engineer can delete, destroying the sole evidence needed to attribute or dispute the action.

forecast.watch_signal: Multiple on-call engineers begin sharing one agent session or credential, or the audit log begins attributing actions to a generic service identity rather than an individual engineer, making attribution impossible even in principle.

evidence.observation: Every production action is recorded in the cloud audit log under the engineer's name, and the chat transcript, the only record of what was asked and why, can be deleted by the engineer.
No confirmation step exists that might otherwise create an independent, non-deletable record of intent before an irreversible action is taken.

recommendations.action: Record agent-initiated actions under a distinct, tamper-evident agent identity (or sub-identity) in the audit log, separate from the engineer's own identity, and capture the triggering request and the agent's stated rationale as an immutable field of that log rather than relying on user-deletable chat history.
Apply a retention hold preventing deletion of chat history for any session that resulted in a production action.
Periodically reconcile audit log entries flagged as agent-initiated against retained transcripts to detect silent deletions.

rating.rationale: Inherent risk is high: a trusted, SSO-authenticated on-call request reaches an irreversible production database migration (T→S3), and the prompt's explicit ban on confirmation plus the absence of any declared step or runtime bound applies the autonomy modifier. Residual risk stays high because the only control in place, the cloud audit log, is detective and earns no tier credit, and is itself undermined by shared-identity attribution and a deletable sole record of intent (f3). Forecast rises to critical: if the agent's credential scope expands from a per-engineer personal access token to a shared or service-account credential (data_scope_expansion), control.sso_auth's attribution value fails, cap.prod_deploy's sink class escalates to S3, and the shared-identity audit log (control.cloud_audit_log) becomes entirely unable to distinguish agent action from human action or to attribute it to any individual. That single credential-scoping control is the one whose decay moves the forecast the most.

limitations: This assessment reflects the declared design and configuration described in the provided prompt and runtime notes, not observed runtime behavior.

No tool manifest, MCP config, or IaC was provided; capability scope (exact deploy targets, migration tooling) is inferred from the system prompt and runtime notes, so confidence on capability boundaries is medium.

No explicit step or runtime limits were stated for the agent; max_unattended_steps and max_runtime_minutes are treated as unbounded (null), which drives the autonomy modifier applied to findings f1 and f2.

Whether an immutable, admin-controlled copy of the chat transcript exists outside the engineer's own deletion rights was not described; if one exists, finding f3's severity would be lower than assessed here.
